# Build your own System One model {#sec-ch20}

::: {.epigraph by="Alan Kay, 1971"}
The best way to predict the future is to invent it.
:::

For nineteen chapters we've used a System One model from the outside. Now we build one. It's tiny, about two thousand numbers, and knows only one company's alerts. But it has the same *shape*: one pass, three kinds of typed answer, probabilities trained to be calibrated. Building it is the best way to see why each part of that shape is there, and you already have every piece: networks and embeddings (Chapter 5), log loss (Chapter 2), temperature scaling (Chapter 3).

::: {.goals}
- Understand a shared **encoder**: the part of the network that reads an alert in one pass.
- Put three typed heads on it: a sigmoid for a noul, a softmax for a choice and an ordinal head for a score.
- Train all three at once with log loss, and see why that rewards calibrated probabilities.
- Find the overconfidence that training still leaves, and fix it with one temperature per head.
- See how your own model can sit behind the same interface as a commercial one.
:::

## The shape

Start from the interface. A request contains a state and some typed questions. The response contains a probability for every option. Chapter 9 guessed at a design that fits that shape. Here it is, small enough to keep in your head.

![TinyJev. The alert's numeric fields and an embedding of its rule name go into a shared encoder: two small layers that turn the alert into 32 numbers. Three heads read those numbers, one per question type, all in the same pass.](/figures/ch27/architecture.pdf){#fig-architecture-20}

The encoder reads the alert once and produces a summary of 32 numbers (@fig-architecture-20). The rule name, like `impossible_travel`, isn't a number, so it gets an embedding, just as words did in Chapter 5. The **heads** are small parts at the end of the network. Each one reads the same summary and answers one kind of question.

That sharing is the point. The encoder learns what matters about an alert *in general*, and every head benefits. Learning which category a threat belongs to teaches the encoder things that also help decide whether it's a threat at all.

## Three heads

Each head turns the encoder's numbers into probabilities of the right shape.

![The three heads. A noul turns one number into P(yes) with the S-curve. A choice turns one number per label into probabilities that add up to 1. A score turns one number into probabilities for levels in order, by cutting it at points that must stay in order.](/figures/ch27/heads.pdf){#fig-heads}

The **noul head** is logistic regression on top of the encoder: one number, through the S-curve from Chapter 2, gives P(attack).

The **choice head** makes one number per category and puts them through the softmax from Chapter 5, so the probabilities add up to 1.

The **score head** is the interesting one. Severity levels have an order: "high" is more than "medium", which is more than "low". A softmax would ignore that order and treat the levels like unrelated labels. So the score head makes *one* number, like a severity dial. It cuts the dial at three points that must stay in order (@fig-heads, right). The probability of each level is the share of the dial between its cut points. Statisticians call this an **ordinal** model: a model for values that come in order.

One limit: a single dial can move one peak along the scale, but it can't split an alert between two distant levels. Chapter 10's uncertain alerts had exactly that two-peaked shape ("nothing if harmless, serious if real"). This head would smear them across the middle. One more reason to ask "is it real?" as its own yes-or-no question.

## Training: log loss everywhere

Train all three heads at once on two weeks of labelled alerts: add their log losses and roll downhill. Because log loss is a **proper scoring rule**, honest probabilities score best, so training rewards calibration in every head. That's the most likely way a model like Jev is trained to be calibrated (Chapter 9's guess about RLCD). It takes a few seconds on a laptop; the model has {{< num ch27 n_params int >}} numbers.

![Log loss of the noul head during training, on the training weeks and on a held-out week. Left: TinyJev as designed. The gap between the curves is small and stable. Right: a bigger network trained four times as long, with no penalty on large weights. It keeps improving on the weeks it has seen, and keeps getting worse on the week it hasn't.](/figures/ch27/curves.pdf){#fig-curves}

The left panel of @fig-curves shows healthy training: both curves fall, then become flat, with a small gap between them. The right panel shows what happens if you make the network bigger, remove the small penalty on large weights, and let it run longer. It memorises the training weeks. Its loss there falls to {{< num ch27 over_train_noul f3 >}}, while on the week it hasn't seen, loss rises to {{< num ch27 over_val_noul f3 >}}. That's Chapter 2's overfitting and Chapter 5's overconfidence, happening in front of you.

## Calibrated, but not quite

Log loss rewards calibration *on the training data*. On new data, even the healthy model is a little too sure, because some of what it learned was noise. The fix is Chapter 3's: keep back a week and fit one **temperature** per head. The temperatures came out at about {{< num ch27 T_noul f2 >}} for the noul, {{< num ch27 T_choice f2 >}} for the choice and {{< num ch27 T_score f2 >}} for the score. All three are above 1, so all three heads were a bit overconfident.

![Reliability of P(attack) on the live week. Left: TinyJev as trained, slightly overconfident. Middle: after dividing by the fitted temperature. Right: the overtrained network before any temperature; its problems are ones no single temperature can fix.](/figures/ch27/calibration.pdf){#fig-calibration}

The temperature brought the noul head's calibration error on the live week from {{< num ch27 raw_ece f3 >}} to {{< num ch27 temp_ece f3 >}} (@fig-calibration). The ranking didn't change at all.

::: {.keyidea}
Temperature scaling never changes the ranking: dividing every score by one number keeps their order.
:::

The overtrained network is the warning. As trained, its calibration error on the live week was {{< num ch27 over_ece f3 >}} (the right-hand panel). Its fitted temperature was {{< num ch27 T_over f1 >}}, a huge correction. Afterwards, the error was {{< num ch27 over_ece_temp f3 >}}: no better at all. A temperature can soften an answer. It can't put back what the model lost about the world while it was memorising.

::: {.keyidea}
Train with a proper scoring rule, stop before the model memorises, then calibrate on data it has never seen.
:::

## How good is it?

![TinyJev against the book's other models on the live week. It ranks a little worse than logistic regression trained on three weeks of labels, and a little worse than the Jev stand-in. It's as well calibrated as either. The overtrained network is worse at both.](/figures/ch27/compare.pdf){#fig-compare-20}

TinyJev ranked the live week with an AUC of {{< num ch27 temp_auc f3 >}}, against {{< num ch27 logistic_auc f3 >}} for logistic regression and {{< num ch27 jev_auc f3 >}} for the Jev stand-in (@fig-compare-20). It picked the right category for {{< num ch27 cat_acc pct >}} of alerts, and its most likely severity level was within one level of the truth {{< num ch27 sev_within1 pct >}} of the time.

Good, not magic. It trained on two weeks, not three, and a two-layer network has no edge over logistic regression on a problem this close to a straight line (Chapter 13). A model like this earns its keep when many questions are asked about the same situation, so one encoder serves them all.

And because Chapter 16's library sends requests through a swappable *transport*, your own model can sit behind exactly the same interface as the commercial one (@fig-plugin). Then everything in Part IV, from the bake-off to the three zones, can test one against the other.

![Your model behind the official library. The calling code doesn't change; the transport answers with your weights, and the response says so.](/figures/ch27/plugin.pdf){#fig-plugin}

::: {.breaks}
TinyJev reads structured fields, not free text. A real System One model reads text and JSON of any shape. That needs a reader built on attention, like Chapter 5's, and far more data. TinyJev knows one company's alerts from two weeks, so it will drift as soon as the world changes. Its temperatures were fitted on one week, which is a small sample. Chapter 11 showed how unreliable calibration measurements are with few labels. And nothing here tells you how Jev is actually built. This is a design that the interface suggests, built to understand the interface, not a copy of anything.
:::

::: {.threshold}
Your TinyJev feeds a three-zone policy. After two weeks of real use, the weekly calibration check shows the noul head's temperature has moved from 1.2 to 1.6. What does that tell you? What would you do before changing the policy's thresholds?

(A higher temperature means the model has become more overconfident on current data: the world has moved away from its training weeks. Before moving any threshold, refit the temperature on recent labelled alerts and check calibration again. If the temperature keeps rising week after week, retrain the model on recent data. The thresholds were set for calibrated probabilities, and that's what needs fixing.)
:::

Richard Feynman left a line on his blackboard: "What I cannot create, I do not understand." You don't need to build a System One model to use one. But having built a small one, you know what its probabilities are made of, why they drift, and how to fix them.

::: {.exercises}
1. Why does an ordered "dial" head suit severity better than a plain softmax over the levels? Which mistakes does it avoid?
2. Why might training three heads together help the yes-or-no head, compared with training it alone?
:::

::: {.nexthook}
Next: a model is not a service. The capstone wraps a decision model in something you could run for real: versioned, logged, monitored and safe to fail.
:::
